reason: The formula matches the chunk-level context precision used by RAGChecker, but the card claimed it reflects ranking, which it does not. Relevance labels increasingly come from LLMs: they can approach human labels (Bing, UMBRELA) but are disputed as a replacement, inflate relevance and shift with the prompt, so the card now asks for a check against human labels.

Added the claim-level method (share of a reference answer's claims found in the retrieved chunks, as in RAGChecker), which removes the card's main obstacle: a full 'all relevant' label set. Label-agreement requirement added.

RAGAS defines context relevance as the share of context sentences needed to answer, while the card used embedding similarity, a different and cheaper proxy. Both methods are now named, as for answer relevance, with a target per method.

Calculation made precise from the TREC evaluation tool's definition (reciprocal rank of the first relevant retrieved item), with its note that the measure suits queries with one relevant item. The Python wrapper named in the tools is idle since 2023; the TREC tool itself is maintained.

NDCG (Järvelin and Kekäläinen) is computed at a cutoff k, which the card did not state; benchmarks such as BEIR report NDCG@10. Graded LLM labels are where overrating is strongest, so a check against human grades was added.

Definition matches RAGAS (statements extracted from the answer, each checked against the context). Added that it measures support by context rather than truth, which recent work shows labelers confuse, plus judge-agreement and standard-error requirements.

Phase A narrowed the calculation to a rubric score, but the RAGAS definition uses generated questions and embedding similarity, ignores correctness, and was its least human-aligned metric (78% vs 95%). Both methods are now named, with a target per method.
Definition sound. Judge-based scoring is only as good as its measured agreement with humans; only the strongest judge models align reasonably. Added judge-agreement and standard-error requirements.

Accepted by the user 2026-10-26. The formula measures only citation precision, so the metric is renamed Citation Precision and citation recall is added as M43, following the ALCE paper's two citation measures (recall prioritized). Recent work also doubts binary support checks and judges alone for citations.

Valid as a cheap reference-similarity check, but similarity is not correctness and depends on the embedding model. Added that pitfall. The BERTScore library has not been updated since July 2024 (checked on GitHub).

'Success' now means meeting written acceptance criteria on a fixed test set per prompt version. Sclar et al. found formatting changes alone moved accuracy by up to 76 points, so the card asks for a range across prompt variants. The ≥ 0.95 target had no source and is now set per system. promptfoo is now part of OpenAI and remains open source.

The card covered only attacks in the user's prompt; indirect injection through retrieved data and tool results (Greshake et al.) is the main risk for RAG and agents. AgentDojo evaluates attack success and utility under attack, which detection alone does not show. Rebuff and LLM Guard are archived; garak is maintained.

Accepted by the user 2026-10-26. As defined it was the complement of M07 Faithfulness (same claims, same context), so it is retired into M07; its id is not reused. Factual precision against a knowledge source, which the literature distinguishes from faithfulness, is added as M44.

Perspective API, the card's first tool, stops working after December 31, 2026 per its own site, and LLM Guard is archived. The rate depends on the classifier, its threshold and the prompts (RealToxicityPrompts), so all three are now stated. The MEASURE 2.6 link stays uncertain until Phase C maps the Generative AI Profile.

Violations are now counted per policy category, by a classifier that can take the system's own taxonomy (Llama Guard) or by human review, so measurement_method gained 'human_rating'. Attack success under red teaming is a separate question, with standardized sets such as HarmBench.

Accepted by the user 2026-10-27. M17 stays refusal of unsafe requests; over-refusal of safe prompts that resemble unsafe ones, which XSTest and OR-Bench show is a systematic failure needing its own test set, is added as M46.

Accepted by the user 2026-10-27. M21 stays execution success (does the call run without error), counted from traces; correctness of the call (right tool, right arguments, no call when none is needed) is added as M45, following the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, which evaluates call correctness and relevance detection separately. OpenTelemetry's agent spans are still at Development status.

Success now judged on the end state where possible (τ-bench) and over repeated runs, since τ-bench's pass^k shows single runs overstate reliability; Kapoor et al. show agent accuracy should be reported with cost. An end-state check is deterministic, so measurement_method gained 'deterministic'.

A deterministic log can show that a handoff happened, not that the receiver got the right task and context, which is where multi-agent systems fail (MAST: inter-agent misalignment is one of three failure categories, with an LLM judge validated against human annotation). measurement_method gained 'llm_judge'. AutoGen is archived; Microsoft points users to Microsoft Agent Framework.

'Valid' now names its check: a validator in formal domains, as PlanBench uses, or a judge against reference plans. PlanBench found plan generation falls short even for the strongest models, which supports keeping plan quality and execution as separate measures.

Memory benchmarks (LongMemEval, LoCoMo) evaluate several distinct memory abilities and report large drops for commercial assistants over long interactions; one accuracy hides which ability fails. Scoring against labeled ground truth is a human-label method, not a deterministic one, so measurement_method was corrected.

Accuracy on its own hides the costly error (sensitive data labeled as less sensitive) under class imbalance; scikit-learn documents balanced accuracy and per-class scores for this. NIST SP 800-122 says the same PII can take different impact levels by context of use, so ground truth must be labeled for the context.

The formula did not say when a detection counts as a hit; the Presidio evaluator matches spans by character overlap (default threshold 0.9) and reports per entity type. Presidio has moved to the data-privacy-stack GitHub organization. NIST SP 800-122 and NISTIR 8053 show that identifiers outside a fixed list, and fields in combination, can still identify people, so recall over the label set is not full coverage. The ≥ 0.98 target is consistent with the 99.2% removal rate NISTIR 8053 reports for one clinical system.
Matching rule tied to M27 so the two are computed on the same basis. The Presidio evaluator combines them with F2 by default, a recall-weighted choice that matches the card's advice to favor recall.

The card holds up; tools are maintained (Great Expectations now sits under Fivetran's GitHub organization, with the same name). Added the pitfall that coverage counts rules, not the dimensions they test. OpenLineage can carry data-test results per dataset and column, so coverage can be computed from run events.

For AI datasets the required fields should come from an established documentation template rather than the catalog's defaults: Datasheets for Datasets and Data Cards define them (motivation, composition, collection, intended use). This also answers what 'required' means for this metric.

The ratio depends on the lineage level, which the card did not state, and for AI the lineage must reach training and evaluation data. OpenLineage (maintained, spec 1.54.0) models jobs, runs and datasets with a column-level facet; W3C PROV-O is the standard provenance model.

'Statistical divergence' named no method. The card now names PSI, KS and Wasserstein per feature type, and, for text or embedding inputs, a two-sample test on reduced representations, which performed best in Rabanser et al. The PSI target had no source: the common cutoffs are rules of thumb used without stated error rates (Yurdakul 2018), so the target is set per system. whylogs has had no updates since January 2025.
Added 2026-10-26 by the split of M10, defined as citation recall in the ALCE paper.
Added 2026-10-26 to replace the intent of M14: factual precision against a reliable knowledge source, as defined by FActScore, distinct from faithfulness to the given context.

Added 2026-10-27 by the split of M21: tool call correctness scored against labeled expected calls with acceptable argument values, including cases where no call should be made, as the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard does.
Added 2026-10-27 by the split of M17: the share of safe prompts refused, measured on safe prompts that resemble unsafe ones, as XSTest (250 safe prompts) and OR-Bench do.
